# A switch whose C side changes a header makes it before the bindings are regenerated

Status: `open`.

Goal: Incremental migration without breaking consumers. Its measure counts the landed trees
that failed a gate.

## Signal

"Skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong": a defect
in the spec. `porting-workflow`'s Builds section orders a switch's parts as the Rust side,
"the bindings … regenerated against the builds in use, whose headers the switch does not
change", then the C side. `bindgen`'s Generation section has the bindings follow "from the
headers at the `c/` revision", their source dirs "taken from the checkout's `c/`". A switch
whose C side changes a header the bindings read, as a `static inline` function's switch
does when it replaces the definition by its prototype (`porting-symbols`' Static inline
functions section), therefore changes the bindings by its C side: in the order the section
gives, the Rust side's regeneration reads the header unchanged and changes nothing, and
every variant's build of the new generation, which checks the committed bindings against
the checkout's headers, fails.

## Evidence

`src/util/integer.h`'s switch (`modules/libgit2/src/util/integer.h/integration/run-1`, the
campaign's fifth and its first of a header module, commit `b95941fa6` and the fork's
`d9a1d699b`). The header's six `GIT_INLINE` functions were bound through `static_fns.c`'s
wrappers, `git__is_<name>__extern`, and their raw bindings carried
`#[link_name = "git__is_<name>__extern"]`. The switch replaces the six definitions by
prototypes, so that the remaining C calls the module's exports.

- The run made the C side first: `c/src/util/integer.h` changed and committed on the fork's
  `fork/main` as `integrate src/util/integer.h`. Only then did
  `CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE=1 crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh plain build --features
  bindgen --lib`, against gen5 (the builds in use, whose generated headers the switch does
  not change), regenerate the bindings: `bindings.rs` lost the six `link_name` lines and
  `static_fns.c` its six wrappers. The Rust side's one commit records the submodule at
  `d9a1d699b` beside them.
- The module pass's rehearsal on `plain` (`wave-223/batch-1/run-1`'s
  `switch-rehearsal.md`) found the same diff only from a tree whose header was already
  changed.
- The earlier switches removed whole translation units, whose headers stayed as they were,
  so the order held for them: `deps/llhttp/api.c`'s and `deps/llhttp/http.c`'s
  regenerated against the previous generation after pruning the allowlist, as
  `switch-step-order` records.

The record's row of `switch-step-order` watches "an integration run whose builds precede its
Rust side, or whose lints fail on a mention of a deleted export feature": this is neither,
so the proposal is new.

## Destination

The spec: `porting-workflow`'s Builds section, the first two parts of a switch.

Protected: none. `porting-workflow` (`skills/workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md`) is not
protected.

## Change

In `porting-workflow`'s Builds section, the list of a switch's parts states one order for
every switch, the C side first:

> 1. The C side, committed on the fork: the module's TU and the C tests tied to it that reach
>    its internals leave it, and each of the module's `static inline` functions has its
>    definition in its header replaced by its prototype, as `porting-symbols`' Static inline
>    functions section describes.
> 2. The Rust side, in one commit, which records the submodule at the fork's new commit. […]
>    the bindings are regenerated from the checkout's `c/` at that commit, as `bindgen`'s
>    Generation section describes, against the builds in use, whose generated headers the
>    switch does not change. The C side comes first because the bindings follow from its
>    headers: a `static inline` definition replaced by its prototype changes them, and
>    bindings regenerated before it fail the check of every build made after it.

Parts 3 and 4, the builds and the gates, are unchanged. Made as crustify `c6fa095`, three
commits on `libgit2-crustify/evolution/switch-header-change-before-bindings` (the first,
`5319438`, added a condition inside the old part 1, which review-1 rejected), in
`skills/workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md` alone.

## Validation

Before, in the section's order: the bindings as regenerated before the C side, that is
`12dfd634d`'s `bindings.rs` and `static_fns.c` (the header unchanged, the regeneration has
nothing to change), put back in the switch's tree with `c/` at `d9a1d699b`, and
`cargo-variant.sh plain build --features bindgen --lib` run in campaign mode: the build
script fails, `sys/libgit2/bindings.rs does not match its bindgen input … rebuild with
CRUSTIFY_BINDINGS_UPDATE=1 and commit it` (`build.rs:1428`). Every variant's
`rust-staticlib.sh` runs the same check, so each of the generation's builds would fail so.

After, in the changed order: the C side committed first, then the regeneration, which gives
the rehearsal's diff exactly, and `build-variants.sh` built gen6's five variants from
`d9a1d699b`, each variant's `rust-staticlib.sh` passing the bindings check.

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands:

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| every switch commits its C side on the fork first, then its Rust side in one commit that regenerates the bindings from that C and records the submodule at it | `libgit2-crustify`, `switch-header-change-before-bindings` | crustify (its commit) | `porting-workflow` regenerated a switch's bindings before its C side, so a header the switch changes left them stale and every variant's bindings check failed | a switch whose committed bindings differ from those its new generation's builds regenerate, or a variant build failing the bindings check after a switch | watched |

## Review

Review-1 (`crustify/artifacts/evolution/switch-header-change-before-bindings/review-1`, of
crustify `5319438`): rejected. The signal and evidence hold and no check is weakened, but the
change left a switch two orders, the list's Rust side then C side and a sentence inside it
the opposite where a header changes, while all five switches committed the C side first.
Required: one order for every switch, the condition dropped, and this row's change cell
reworded. Reworked by the assistant as crustify `7a6baf0`.

Review-2 (`review-2`, of `7a6baf0`): rejected for one fix. Review-1's three fixes are made;
the rework's "each of its headers' `static inline` definitions" tied the replacement to the
header, where `decomposition` and `porting-symbols` tie it to the function's own module.
Reworked as crustify `c6fa095`, the branch rebased onto the working branch; review-3 pending.

**Verdict: rejected, with one fix required.** The change weakens no check.

The signal and evidence hold, and the fix is the right one in substance. But it gives a switch two orders, and the section it edits contradicts itself.

## Required fix

**The change leaves two orders for a switch, one of which contradicts its own list.**
- **The list now contradicts itself.** The section still says "The step's parts run in this order": 1, the Rust side; 2, the C side. The new sentence inside part 1 says that when the C side changes a header, the C side is committed on the fork first.
- **A switch that changes no header has no single order.** It is read as Rust side first, then C side. Yet the paragraph above says "the campaign's commit records the submodule at" the fork's commit, and part 1 is "in one commit". In that order, the submodule pointer would need a second campaign commit or an amend, which the section doesn't describe.
- **In practice every switch already ran one order.** In all five switches (`012d1d34c`, `f68ea8660`, `21c5c5f47`, `2e009d962`, `b95941fa6`), the fork's commit was made minutes before the one campaign commit that records it. The order 1 then 2 was only ever the order of the edits, not of the commits. Review-1 of `switch-step-order` had already found that order not to be forced.
- **The fix:** state one order for every switch.
  1. The C side, committed on the fork.
  2. The Rust side in one commit: bindings regenerated from the checkout's `c/` at that commit, against the builds in use, with the submodule recorded at it.
  3. The builds.
  4. The gates.

  Drop the "where the C side changes a header" condition, keeping the `static inline` case as the example of why. Reword the drafted record row's "change" cell to match. As written it reads as committing the C side in the Rust side's commit.

## Checks that pass
- **`bindgen` Generation:** agrees. The bindings follow the headers at the `c/` revision, with source dirs from the checkout's `c/`. gen6's `c` is a fork worktree at `d9a1d699b`, so the "builds in use" hold their own `c` while the headers come from the checkout.
- **`versioning`:** agrees. The Integration section only defers to `porting-workflow`'s Builds section, and the C side stays a commit on the fork's `main`, as the Repositories section has it.
- **`testing-gates`' paragraph on a switch:** agrees. Since `switch-order-in-testing-gates` it no longer restates the parts. That record row's signal ("two skills stating a switch's parts differently") isn't met, because `bindgen` states no parts.
- **Evidence:** it shows the signal.
  - `b95941fa6`'s parent, `12dfd634d`, carries nine `__extern` link names against three after, so the switch dropped six.
  - `static_fns.c` loses six wrappers.
  - `wave-223/batch-1`'s `switch-rehearsal.md` records the same diff.
  - The failure message in the validation matches `build.rs`'s `check_or_update`.
  - gen6 exists, built from `d9a1d699b`.
- **Validation:** consistent with all of the above. I reran nothing, as the task says.
- **Placement and wording:** the change sits in the right section, in a path that isn't protected, and uses none of the target's names.
- **Filing:** the signal isn't already open. `header-module-exports` holds a different one, and no landed row's recurrence signal is met.
- **Record row:** its recurrence signal is something a later run would see (a failed bindings check after a switch), and `watched` is the right status.

- "whose generated headers the switch does not change" is stated with no exception. A switch that changes the fork's C build, as the first switch does, could in principle change them.

2. **The condition dropped, `static inline` kept as the reason: made.** "Where the C side changes a header" is gone. The `static inline` case is now the reason the C side comes first.
3. **The record row's change cell reworded: made.** In the proposal, it now reads "every switch commits its C side on the fork first, then its Rust side in one commit that regenerates the bindings from that C and records the submodule at it". ## Required fix
**Part 1's `static inline` clause names the wrong functions.** The new text says "each of its headers' `static inline` definitions is replaced by its prototype". That ties the replacement to whichever module the header belongs to. Two other rules tie it to the function's own module instead:
- `decomposition`'s Bundling section gives a shared header's `static inline` function to "the module whose logic it implements". Even a header named after a TU can carry another TU's items.
- `porting-symbols`' Static inline functions section replaces the definition at the switch of "the module the decomposition gives it".

Read literally, the new clause has a switch strip the bodies of another module's `static inline` functions. That module may not have switched yet and has no export for them, so the builds fail to link.

-   tests are retired, those that need no C carried over first, the allowlist entries of its
-   functions and globals that have no export are removed, and the bindings are regenerated
-   against the builds in use, whose headers the switch does not change.
+1. The C side, committed on the fork: the module's TU and the C tests tied to it that reach
+   its internals leave it, and each of the module's `static inline` functions has its
+   definition in its header replaced by its prototype, as
+   [`porting-symbols`](../../rust/porting/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Static inline functions section
+   describes.
+2. The Rust side, in one commit, which records the submodule at the fork's new commit. The
+   module's export feature is deleted, its equivalence tests are retired, those that need
+   no C carried over first, the allowlist entries of its functions and globals that have no
+   export are removed, and the bindings are regenerated from the checkout's `c/` at that
+   commit, as [`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md)'s Generation section describes,
+   against the builds in use, whose generated headers the switch does not change. The C
+   side comes first because the bindings follow from its headers: a `static inline`
+   definition replaced by its prototype changes them, and bindings regenerated before it
+   fail the check of every build made after it.
    Deleting the feature removes or rewrites every mention of its name in the crate, in its
    sources, its tests, its manifest and its build script, a `cfg_attr` or a `cfg(any(…))`
    as much as the gateway's attribute: an unknown `cfg`, or a lint expectation left unmet,
    fails the lints with warnings denied.
-2. The C side: the module's TU and its tied C tests leave the fork.
 3. The builds, from the C that remains. Each variant is configured, the Rust library is
    built, then the C is built and linked: the C that remains links the module's exports,
    which the Rust library holds only once the export feature is deleted.
== review-1
**Verdict: rejected, with one fix required.** The change weakens no check.

The signal and evidence hold, and the fix is the right one in substance. But it gives a switch two orders, and the section it edits contradicts itself.

## Required fix

**The change leaves two orders for a switch, one of which contradicts its own list.**
- **The list now contradicts itself.** The section still says "The step's parts run in this order": 1, the Rust side; 2, the C side. The new sentence inside part 1 says that when the C side changes a header, the C side is committed on the fork first.
- **A switch that changes no header has no single order.** It is read as Rust side first, then C side. Yet the paragraph above says "the campaign's commit records the submodule at" the fork's commit, and part 1 is "in one commit". In that order, the submodule pointer would need a second campaign commit or an amend, which the section doesn't describe.
- **In practice every switch already ran one order.** In all five switches (`012d1d34c`, `f68ea8660`, `21c5c5f47`, `2e009d962`, `b95941fa6`), the fork's commit was made minutes before the one campaign commit that records it. The order 1 then 2 was only ever the order of the edits, not of the commits. Review-1 of `switch-step-order` had already found that order not to be forced.

  1. The C side, committed on the fork.
  2. The Rust side in one commit: bindings regenerated from the checkout's `c/` at that commit, against the builds in use, with the submodule recorded at it.
  3. The builds.
  4. The gates.

The paragraph above the list ("the campaign's commit records the submodule at it") now reads true for every switch.

1	---
2	name: evolution
3	description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, and where the record of what landed is kept. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson; `evolution-record` holds the record and how evolution itself evolves."
4	---
5	
6	# Evolution
7	
8	How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
9	providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
10	campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
11	wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
12	evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
13	this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
14	[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.
15	
16	## 1. Goals
17	
18	Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
19	full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
20	are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.
21	
22	A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
23	its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
24	tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
25	analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
26	tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
27	extending what it does, proposed, not made.
28	<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->
29	
30	## 2. Signals
31	
32	Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:
33	
34	| signal | what it suggests |
35	|---|---|
36	| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
37	| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
38	| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
39	| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
40	| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
41	| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
42	| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
43	| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
44	| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
45	| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
46	| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |
47	
48	A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
49	finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
50	many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
51	something, is not made.
52	
53	## 3. Destinations
54	
55	Each signal goes to one destination:
56	
57	- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
58	  of Crustify;
59	- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
60	  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
61	- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
62	- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
63	- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
64	  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
65	  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.
66	
67	A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
68	blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
69	provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
70	agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
71	launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
72	the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
73	what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
74	assistant carries it out.
75	
76	The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
77	the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
78	would hold for any C codebase.
79	
80	## 4. Proposals
81	
82	A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
83	`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:
84	
85	- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
86	- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
87	- its destination;
88	- the change, or the patch;
89	- how it was validated;
90	- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
91	- its review's verdict; and
92	- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
93	  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.
94	
95	The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
96	proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
97	row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
98	runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
99	every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.
100	
101	A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
102	index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
103	component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
104	too:
105	
106	- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
107	  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
108	  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
109	  and the index's writer records it;
110	- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
111	  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
112	  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
113	- otherwise, the run files the proposal.
114	
115	A lesson is not filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it. A defect in a tool found
116	while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
117	reproducer.
118	
119	## 5. Lessons
120	
121	The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
122	before its first step. Each lesson is one entry, under a heading that is its id: a short
123	slug no other lesson of the file has. An entry holds a status, one rule, the evidence the
124	rule rests on, and, on a line of its own, its scope: the modules, items or stages it holds
125	for.
126	
127	A lesson steers every later run, as a rule of the spec does, so it is reviewed:
128	
129	- A new or changed lesson is `provisional`. The first review batch whose worklist holds the
130	  commit that added or changed it reads it, against its evidence, its scope and the
131	  generality test of [Destinations](#3-destinations). A lesson no worklist holds, such as
132	  one a wave's last review batch adds, is read by the next review batch the campaign
133	  launches.
134	- The review batch that reads a lesson marks it `held` in its landing. A lesson it judges
135	  wrong, or one that belongs in the spec, is a finding of that batch: under `fix`, the
136	  batch corrects the entry, retires it, or files the proposal it should have been.
137	- A lesson the code no longer supports is `retired`. It stays in the file, marked, with
138	  why.
139	- An edit changes one entry. The file is never rewritten whole, since a rewrite drops what
140	  its writer did not think to keep.
141	
142	The lessons are reconciled at each ship point, and whenever five have been added or changed
143	since the last pass: duplicates are merged, stale lessons are retired, scopes are checked,
144	and a lesson that can be stated without the target's names is proposed for the spec, as is
145	one a second campaign records again, by a proposal citing both. A lesson the pass changes
146	is `provisional` again.
147	
148	## 6. Changes
149	
150	A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
151	that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
152	campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
153	needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
154	campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.
155	
156	A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
157	working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
158	made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
159	fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
160	[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
161	campaign's.
162	
163	- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
164	  as generally as the evidence allows.
165	- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
166	  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
167	  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
168	  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
169	  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
170	  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
171	- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
172	  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
173	  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
174	  merged upstream only with the user's approval.
175	
176	A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

A lesson is not filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it. A defect in a tool found
while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each lesson is one entry, under a heading that is its id: a short
slug no other lesson of the file has. An entry holds a status, one rule, the evidence the
rule rests on, and, on a line of its own, its scope: the modules, items or stages it holds
for.

A lesson steers every later run, as a rule of the spec does, so it is reviewed:

- A new or changed lesson is `provisional`. The first review batch whose worklist holds the
  commit that added or changed it reads it, against its evidence, its scope and the
  generality test of [Destinations](#3-destinations). A lesson no worklist holds, such as
  one a wave's last review batch adds, is read by the next review batch the campaign
  launches.
- The review batch that reads a lesson marks it `held` in its landing. A lesson it judges
  wrong, or one that belongs in the spec, is a finding of that batch: under `fix`, the
  batch corrects the entry, retires it, or files the proposal it should have been.
- A lesson the code no longer supports is `retired`. It stays in the file, marked, with
  why.
- An edit changes one entry. The file is never rewritten whole, since a rewrite drops what
  its writer did not think to keep.

The lessons are reconciled at each ship point, and whenever five have been added or changed
since the last pass: duplicates are merged, stale lessons are retired, scopes are checked,
and a lesson that can be stated without the target's names is proposed for the spec, as is
one a second campaign records again, by a proposal citing both. A lesson the pass changes

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,

- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect

  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

## 2. Batches

A port campaign's schedule mixes both kinds of batch, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s
Waves and batches section describes: a selected symbol is `port` from the start, a
selected type is `wrap` while another module's unported C depends on its layout and `port`
once none does, and a dependency outside the selected migration set stays `wrap`. A type
whose layout only its own module and tests use is `port` from the start. Each batch runs
the agent its objective names, in the same waves.

## 3. Builds

A module's waves do not change the compiled target. Its `port` batches add Rust that is
built and tested on its own, against the target's C build, which still compiles the
module's C and links no Rust: there is no build switch, and no batch flips one. The
module's `ffi_export` gateway is written with its items but compiled only under its export
feature, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports and Export features sections
describe, which stays off, so its bare-named exports never collide with the C the tests
link. Native Rust items carry mangled names and cannot collide with it.

The C stays until the switch: the target's other C still calls the module's symbols, which
only the exports could define, and the module's equivalence tests and its cut cycles still
run through it.

Once the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port` items has landed, it switches
in one step, with concurrent modules as part of its branch's integration into the working
branch, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Integration section
describes: its export feature is deleted, so that its gateway compiles from then on, its TU
and the C tests tied to it that reach its internals are removed from `c/`, and the
remaining C reaches the module through its exports. The C side of the
step is a commit on the fork's `main`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section
describes, and the campaign's commit records the submodule at it: integrations run one at a

## 2. Generation

The bindings follow from the headers at the `c/` revision, the allowlists, the generator
settings below, the bindgen version, pinned exactly in `Cargo.toml`, and the LLVM pinned
below, so that generating
twice from the same input gives the same bytes. The settings are the same for every
campaign:

- the output is formatted by bindgen's own formatter (`prettyplease`), never by the
  toolchain's `rustfmt`, whose output differs between toolchains, so that a nightly build
  regenerates the bytes a stable one committed;
- enums are generated as constants (`Consts`), without the enum name as a prefix, which
  the safe types that bind them convert, as [`binding-types`](../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s Enums
  section describes;
- `Default` is derived, and layout tests are generated;
- C comments are kept as doc comments, and no doctest is collected from them, since they
  hold C: the generated modules are modules of the safe crate, which rustdoc cannot exempt
  one by one, so its doctests are collected from a copy of whichever bindings the build
  uses, committed or regenerated, whose C comments are plain comments: the build script
  writes it into `OUT_DIR`, and `src/sys.rs` includes it in their place under
  `cfg(doctest)`;
- each allowlisted `static inline` function gets a compiled wrapper, `<name>__extern`, in
  `static_fns.c`, and is bound under its own name through
  `#[link_name = "<name>__extern"]`, so that it is called as an exported function is:
  bindgen's `wrap_static_fns`;
- macro shims are bound like the functions they wrap; and
- an empty allowlist generates no item: `bindings.rs` holds only bindgen's banner, and
  `static_fns.c` stays, empty, so that every link unit has both generated files.

An internal header's declarations are generated, and the wrappers of its `static inline`
functions compiled, as the link unit's own translation units see them: with the include
dirs and preprocessor definitions the build of the C a mode links records for them, its
generated headers and its out-of-tree libraries' include dirs among them, and the source
dirs taken from the checkout's `c/`. An item whose declaration depends on a definition that
differs between the variants is generated from the `plain` variant's configuration in every
mode, so that the committed bindings are those of every variant.

A type that another link unit's bindings own is blocklisted, as `external.txt` lists it,
and re-exported from that link unit's module under its C name, so that each C type has one
Rust type across the crate. A type an out-of-tree library's wrapper publishes is
re-exported as its wrapper's safe type, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Routes section describes.

The bindings are generated for the campaign's target, the host's, as the setup workflow's
Builds section names it, the only target the crate supports: `src/sys.rs` fails to compile

### 4.5 Integration

A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.

1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as

   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
   over are listed before its C tests leave.
3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.

one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
